title: A Giant Icy World Hiding Beyond Pluto
summary: Astronomers may have found a new world at the edge of our solar system. The object is called 2026 ED138 for now. Matthew Holman spotted it on October 13, using the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Mario Juric of the University of Washington helped check the find. Holman used software made with Kevin Napier to scan billions of pictures for tiny moving points of light. Juric found 20 more sightings, some from March 2026, and older pictures going back to 2016. ED138 is now about 46 astronomical units from the Sun, while Pluto averages about 40. The object is about 1,000 kilometres across, the biggest world found beyond Neptune in about 20 years. If confirmed, it would be our sixth dwarf planet, joining Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. Scientists think an icy object this big is probably round, but they need more looks to be sure. It stayed hidden in a crowded patch of sky near the Milky Way, where millions of stars hid its faint movement.
why_it_matters: Learning about new worlds far from the Sun can help you understand how big our solar system is and how scientists keep discovering things beyond what you learn in school.

background_read: Our solar system has the Sun and worlds that travel around it, including planets and smaller dwarf planets far away.
Pluto is one dwarf planet that travels far from the Sun, beyond Neptune.
Astronomers look for tiny moving points of light in sky pictures to find new faraway worlds that are hard to see.
Article_Structure: WHO: Matthew Holman, Mario Juric and Kevin Napier, astronomers who searched sky pictures for the new world.
WHAT: They may have found a large icy world called 2026 ED138 beyond Pluto that could become our sixth dwarf planet.
WHERE: At the edge of our solar system, about 46 astronomical units from the Sun, in a crowded patch of sky near the Milky Way.
WHY: They need more looks to check if the icy object is round and confirm it as a dwarf planet.
